utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start, a few procedural matters. First of all, I was informed that the Defence would like to respond to the Prosecution's response to the -- well, let's say Rule 68 motion. The Chamber's inclined, has briefly discussed the matter, to grant such a request if it would be made, but if the Prosecution would strongly object against it, we'd like to hear it now. And when I say "strongly object," that means that we'd prefer to -- but within certain limits. That means, I take it, Mr. Josse, that going to the core of the case and leaving out all the niceties and what the history is and what again was the date of the filing. Just go to the qualification and be done within three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. The original motion wasn't very long, as Your Honours probably observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Three pages would do?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would there be any objection against a three-page response to the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We initially -- we do object, but when you characterise it as whether we strongly object, of course we can't frame it that way. We do obviously reserve, if there are no issues raised in the course of the pleading by Defence counsel reserve the right to respond to any new arguments that have not been raised previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would not expect that, because of course we would get into a tradition where a response to a response would introduce all kind of new matters apart from perhaps some details. Then of course the Chamber might be less disinclined next time to decline grant such requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, absolutely. And might I say in passing, I was going to inquire as to what happened to the Prosecution's application for an extension of one day under Rule 27 -- 127. I assume that was granted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We should -- perhaps we should have asked you, but I think as a matter of fact -- I don't know whether it's assigned already, but on these kind of matters we're trying to be practical just as I am now being practical for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It takes more time to argue on whether these three pages could be submitted, yes or no, and at the same time the parties have some understanding on that this kind of, I would say, flexibility. I'm not talking about generosity should not result in new issues to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't wish to take that technical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you. Then what is not yet requested is nevertheless granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We are grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is, respond three pages. Then I do understand that P1166, P1168, P1147, P1092 are ready to be submitted, at least the translations are ready to be submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then as usual, the Defence has got one week to object against these translations, and otherwise they are admitted into evidence, and the provisional admissions of the original will become a final -- a final admission. Then I do understand that the five lines of the 1st of January, 1992 telephone conversation have been -- has been freshly translated. The parties have received it. If there's -- they have not received that yet. Then you'll receive it very soon, I take it. Yes. And once you've received it, please let me know whether there's any further reason to -- to take up this issue. Again, if not, the original lines will be replaced by these five -- I shouldn't say lines; it's boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then a final issue is the following: Mr. Krajisnik received the -- the floppy disk that was seized at the time of his arrest and which stayed in the hands of the Prosecution for quite some time. Mr. Harmon, Mr. Krajisnik would like to provide to Defence counsel the printout of the list of files appearing on that floppy disk. I take it that since you've seized it and have used it for whatever investigations you would like, that you are aware, at least, of what the content of that floppy disk was and whether there is any problem if at this stage of the proceedings Mr. Krajisnik would provide just a list of files on the floppy disk to Defence counsel. If you say I'd first like to check to know exactly whether what was on it before you'd respond ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yeah, the correspondence. I had a correspondence with Defence counsel about what had been seized from Mr. Krajisnik at the time of his arrest. I frankly put that correspondence aside, and I haven't refreshed my recollection with it, so I will do so after the first break, and then I'll be in better position to inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, you've heard this, so let's wait for at least a couple of hours to see whether the Prosecution would have any objection against this. Would you mind if I provide a copy of what you printed out to the Prosecution, because the Prosecution has had access to the floppy disks for many, many years. So to say, well, they shouldn't see it as perhaps -- even -- yes. Mr. Harmon, perhaps that may assist you in choosing your position. That's what Mr. Krajisnik would like to ... So we'll hear from you on the matter. And then as soon as we have heard from the Prosecution, Mr. Krajisnik, we'll decide whether you're allowed to give this list Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we seem to be in a rather odd position now. The Prosecution have been given the list, and if they object now to us having the list, they've had and we haven't. It seems a rather odd result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you shouldn't have it, but then of course the next issue would be that whether the fact that Mr. Krajisnik got it back only now, I mean, the issue is whether it should be given to you during the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's been given to the Prosecution now in the course of the examination, Your Honour. I take it Mr. Harmon will say we can just have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll make a copy of this, or if a copy of this can be made, I'll just give this to Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's just matter of communication, witness and Defence counsel at this moment. But Mr. Harmon has already said that he has no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Problem solved, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be provided to you at this very moment by Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that matter has been resolved as well. Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, that you would speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examination by Mr. Stewart [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just before the adjournment yesterday evening there was mention of the Law on Internal Affairs. That has been previously exhibited as P64, binder 21, tab 598. I wonder if Mr. Krajisnik could have that, please. That's the B/C/S number, and there's the point 1 number translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I take it you want to refer to P64A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did I not say that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I might have done. Yes. It's P64A, Your Honour, thank you. Binder 21, tab 598.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we can see it's the Law on Internal Affairs. We should be able to save ourselves looking at the first 125 articles. If we can go to very near the end and pick it up at Article 126. It will be in the last couple of pages. It's on the very last page of your version in your language.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Stewart may wish to move the lectern away from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've done that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Article 126, Mr. Krajisnik? You'll follow it in your own language. "Centres for public security services and public security stations of the Ministry of the Interior of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the territory of the Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be closed from the day the present law comes into force and shall resume their work as organising units of the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in accordance with the present law." And then we should look at Article 127.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters request, we do not have the text of the law and it's a bit awkward to interpret off-the-cuff the language of the law. Maybe we could put it on the ELMO or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: My apologies. Your Honour, I have a spare copy in B/C/S myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could put it on the ELMO so the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Last page I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- five articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's all on the last page in the Serbian, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've still got your own printed copy, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Article 127 reads: "Serb employees, other employees from administrations in the seat of the Ministry of the Interior of SRBiH who express their wish and employees of the closed centres of public security services and public security stations who were employed at these centres on the day the present law came into force shall be transmitted to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." I won't trouble with Article 28 [as interpreted], which could be regarded as consequential, but it -- important but it's to do with the transfer over of equipment, so it's consistent with those other provisions. Then Article 129, which we had looked at briefly yesterday. "General acts on internal organisation of the ministry and the public security services shall be enacted within 15 days from the day the present law has entered into effect." And 130: "The present law shall enter into effect eight days after its publication in the Official Gazette of the Serb People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And it's signed by you as president of the Assembly. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik is it -- from that reading it's clear to you what Article 126 and Article 127 together are purporting to do, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- and Article 130, we can leave 129 for a minute, but Article 130: "The present law shall enter into effect eight dates after its publication in the Official Gazette." We have checked this, Mr. Krajisnik. This was published in the Official Gazette number 4 on the 23rd of March, 1992. So that simple arithmetic in accordance with Article 130, the law was to enter into effect on the 31st of March, 1992. First of all, do you -- take it from me, Mr. Krajisnik, certainly at least for the moment, that there was that publication on the 23rd of March, 1992. Is there any reason to suppose that it was not then to come into effect on the 31st of March as I've just summarised it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that this dispatch was dispatched in an unauthorised manner. The Ministry of the Interior has its minister, and the minister, as you could see, was nominated and accepted by the president of the government, that is by the prime minister, only on the 24th of March, the day after the promulgation. This law could not have been implemented without the government, because it wasn't adopted by the government. And you skipped Article 29 [sic], which states that both the rules of the procedure of the ministry and the security service have to be adopted within 15 days of its entry into force, and those rules are something that the minister has to endorse based on a draft proposed by the government, and the government couldn't have done that because it was only established on the 15th of May. So the entire subject of the discussion was this dispatch. The man who sent it testified here, and he said clearly that he was instructed to make this dispatch by Mico Stanisic. Mico Stanisic was here in The Hague. He's now on provisional release. He probably gave a statement to the OTP, and he needs to confirm whether he indeed made such instructions or this witness did it on his own initiative. All the more so, because a reference here is made to Ugljevik, whereas I know for certain that Bijeljina was in play. Nobody knew about it. And just one more thing. While we were at the conference, prime minister was at Pale. He was able to consult both the minister and others about whether this dispatch needed to be sent. I'm not sure about the minister of interior, though, because maybe he was replaced by Delimustafic by that time. You can check all that in the documentation. It's verifiable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you -- did you in March 1992 personally study the details of this Law on Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. It was only supposed to serve as political pressure, because in the Cutileiro Plan, in the negotiations about the Cutileiro Plan, it was envisaged that we have power over the Ministry of the Interior. We had already agreed with the other side about that, and it was supposed to send a message you cannot go back on this. I think I read about it here in The Hague already when Witness Mandic testified, and even then I didn't read all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, because it might cause confusion later at page 8, line 12, it says Mr. Krajisnik did in fact say Article 29, but it's plain that he meant 129.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that -- is that as plain -- could you please -- because Article 29 also deals with a --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, not -- Your Honour, it was -- I suggest it was very plain from what he then went on to say that he meant --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you meant 129, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a slip of the tongue. I certainly meant 129, because that's what I see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript's accurate, Your Honour. It was a slip of the tongue by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Krajisnik, given what you said yesterday about the shock that came to those of you in Brussels when the piece of paper came in indicating the step that had been taken by Mr. Mandic, was there then any communication directly or indirectly subsequently from those who had been in Brussels to Mr. Mandic in relation to what he'd just done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't contact Mr. Mandic. I wasn't in touch with him. I don't remember what Mr. Karadzic did, but I know he was upset and anxious, and he wanted to check with somebody whether it was really an authentic facsimile, an authentic dispatch or a forgery. All participants can confirm what I'm saying, because this dispatch caused us great trouble in the negotiations as I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm still a bit wondering about when a law takes effect when government have to adopt or -- I don't know exactly what Mr. Krajisnik said, but that the government would have to -- let me just check what he literally said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- well, it's just after that reference to Article 29 or that -- that -- that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you guide me to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. It's line 12 on page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm adding to the confusion if I say Article 29 because of course I mean Article 129 as was intended. Yes, and it's Rules, not "rusle" obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On page 8, line 13, you say this law could not have been implemented without the government because it wasn't adopted by the government. Please correct me when I'm wrong. I always understood the legislative procedure to be that the government or minister would send the proposal to the Assembly, that Assembly would then adopt that, and that Rules would be made for when such a law would take effect. Now, I see, if I'm well informed, but otherwise we should perhaps look at what we find on the 23rd of March. Could Madam Usher give us the top of this document on the ELMO so that this, prior to 1, the very beginning of the document, where it starts. Yes. Yes. I understood this to be that in the Official Gazette of the 23rd of March, effect was given was to a law of which the text had been adopted on the 28th of February. But perhaps we'll first invite the interpreters to translate everything that's on the heading so that we know at least what it says. Could we have the translation starting under number 28. Perhaps English first. I don't -- do you have it on the screen? Has the booth --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Are we expected to do an on-site translation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I could ask someone to read it and then you would translate it. Perhaps Mr. Krajisnik, if you would slowly read what this text says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And later I would like to explain something. I think I can be of great assistance in clarifying this entire problem. And now I'm going to read. "Pursuant to Article 80, paragraph 4 of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in connection with Article -- Article not stated, paragraph 2 of the constitutional law for the implementation of the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, acting presidents of the Republic hereby adopt this decree proclaiming the Law on Internal Affairs. The Law on Internal Affairs enacted by the National Assembly at its session of the 28th of February, 1992, is here by promulgated. Number 02-100/92. 28 February 1992. Sarajevo. Acting presidents of the Republic, Dr. Biljana Plavsic, in her own hand; Dr. Nikola Koljevic, in his own hand." That is the first part that you wanted me to read and that you can see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore it's not clear to me yet that where the law is promulgated a couple of weeks after it has been adopted, where the law gives a clear indication of when it will take effect, that's eight days after publication, being on the 23rd of March, that you say there's -- nevertheless, it has to be accepted by the government. And the basis for that is not entirely clear. And since we'd like to fully understand your answer in that respect, I invite you to give the explanation that you announced you were able to give.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you could just look at Article 25. It is linked with -- it is related to Article 29. I can read this Article 25 if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have the English translation of Article 25. And on the P64A, tab 5, 198, the heading was not reflected in English, although I think in one of the other versions of the same document it was. But here 25 is translated on paper. So there's no need to -- to read it aloud. We can see in front of us what it says. Perhaps 25 should remain on the ELMO. Yes. We have the English translation in front of us, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says in Article 29 that: "Within not more than 15 days from the entry into force of that law, general enactments shall be passed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we keep getting these references, to 29 when it should be 129. It's going to be -- Your Honour, once again, it's clear. I take Your Honour's point. It's clear from what Mr. Krajisnik has just said that he is meaning 129. It's going to cause a lot of confusion if we don't get that straight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm saying 129.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters beg to differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there is a mistake. And where earlier you said -- because -- I wouldn't say there is of course the famous play the comedy of errors, but this of course is not a comedy. You referred --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot understand that I can be mistaken all this time. 129 is what I mean. It says there that the Rules of Procedure shall be adopted within 15 days. That's Article 29. And Article 25 says that that -- those Rules of Procedure shall be adopted by the minister at the proposal of the government, whereas the government didn't exist at that moment. It wasn't only formed on the 15th of May. Particularly in view of the fact that there was a political reason behind all this. It was not the intention for an unauthorised person to send -- to send a dispatch. There are other things wrong with this as well. You will find security centres here. In the -- in the law it's Ugljevik, and in the dispatch -- in the law it's Bijeljina, and in the dispatch it's Ugljevik. I really don't know why the man sent it the way he did, but this law could not have been put into practice without the government, without the minister. And this man could not have overridden the entire organisation. All of this had to be endorsed by the government so that the entire organisation be valid. And it was later indeed adopted by the government once the government was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I understand you well, you say Article 25 tells us that the -- at least and I'm quoting the text, that internal structure of the national security services, that they should be determined by special ordinance and that it should be the minister who shall enact the aforementioned ordinance with the government's consent. So there we find in Article 25, first and second paragraph, we find, and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Other rules cannot be adopted without the government either. Everything is said in the dispatch. The organisation is there, security, everything. And it was not carried out in accordance with the dispatch, so what happened was just a great deal of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, just because I might have forgotten, then at a later stage this was enacted? You tell us. Do you remember when approximately this was? And I don't know whether it's in evidence yet, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the beginning of April. Three or four days later, the war broke out. There was chaos then, and there was no effect involved whatsoever, positive or negative. Peace conferences were held, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you say as far as the content is concerned, that -- that ordinance was of a different character compared is to what we find in the dispatch sent by Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ugljevik instead of Bijeljina. That's what he put. He mentioned a centre which does not exist. Your Honours, just one small matter by your leave. The official minister, Mr. Delimustafic, immediately sent a dispatch to all the centres, and he said that this was invalid, and he sent a dispatch stating that Mr. Mandic had been removed from office. But for two or three days, this went all over Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then compare -- I don't know to what extent all this is in evidence, but we'll try to fine the relevant documents and -- so as to better understand your testimony. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, we can go straight to that very document that Mr. Krajisnik was referring to, which is already in evidence as P421.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, well, first of all, can you glance at that and say is that the document that you were referring to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we had this document when Mr. Mandic testified. But even then I hadn't read it in detail. If it's necessary for me to read it in detail, then I need time. However, I know that that document was there at the time. I think it was the Prosecution that presented it to Mr. Mandic. I'm not sure, but I think that it was the Prosecution that presented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you're right about that, Mr. Krajisnik. And we probably don't need to look at every line of it, but it's 31st of March, 1992, addressed to MUP administrations or SDB security service, CSB security services centre, chief Sarajevo SUP, secretariat of the interior, SJB public security station. It's all chief police stations, all commander. It may be not exactly the same, but similarly to Mr. Mandic's document it's been given very wide circulation within the MUP and related are began. It says: "In very complex security conditions in the Republic in which there is a need to secure the unity and coordinated action of the state organs, especially the MUP, we have witnessed various attempts to break the unity of the ministry and even workers in charge succumbing to various foreign influences and daily politics. How destructive this is to the unity of the MUP is testified to by the dispatch sent to you by the UZSK crime prevention administration, number given, 31 March, 1992, which was signed by assistant minister Momcilo Mandic. One hardly need say anything about the contents of the dispatch in view of the existing legal system taking into consideration all the current dilemmas pointed out in the dispatch to workers of the MUP of a certain nationality, I am unable to dwell more closely with the --" the next word appears to be illegible, Mr. Krajisnik. It says, the something. It quotes. I don't know whether you're able to decipher that word.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read on, so I wasn't really following what you were reading. Could you just tell me what part of the text you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the reference to Mr. Mandic. It's a just a couple of sentences on. It says: "I am unable to dwell more closely with the --" and then can you read the next few words, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should say, "regulations that it invokes," but a letter is missing, P. It should be "propisje," regulations that it invokes. The reference is to the dispatch. What I have here in Serbian is just the letter P, but the meaning should be "propisje," regulations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Because they are unknown to any of the professional services in the MUP nor were they presented to me by anyone, not even by the workers in charge whose names are mentioned in the dispatch. Unfortunately, they are my advisor and assistant. Obviously these are problems in the leadership and, therefore, I appeal to all ministry workers to stay out of and above them and to continue," and if you're there, Mr. Krajisnik, what are the next few words, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be "izvrsavanja." Probably "expression." No, it should be "izvrsavanja," which means carrying out very responsible and honourable duties. So it just said "is" and it should be "izvrsavanja." The entire word should be there and only the first two letters are there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then continues: "Very responsible and honourable work and tasks entrusted to them in the existing organisation of the MUP. Finally, I would like to take this opportunity to again express my belief that the greatest number of MUP workers wish to work in a united MUP and that they find any segregation, especially on a national basis, difficult. Do not allow anyone to separate you from your work colleagues, because there are countless examples of mutual solidarity and sacrifice for others in carrying out security tasks even in conditions in which their execution endangers one's own life. I believe the problems are current and the fruit of manipulation by the ill intentioned because there are no difficulties approximately 10.000 of us workers cannot resolve successfully through unified, professional, and lawful work. Inform all MUP workers of the contents of the dispatch. Minister of the Interior, Alija Delimustafic." And I won't for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, unless somebody insists I do, I won't read the -- what appears to be the attachment which doesn't carry the central points any further for immediate purposes. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, did you become aware of the existence of this document at or very shortly after the time it was apparently circulated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, together we tried to deal with the misunderstandings. When I say "we," I mean the two sides. But reasons were put forth by both sides. This is a demagogic approach on the part of Mr. Alija Delimustafic, the minister. Because irrespective of the dispatch that was sent without authorisation, in the Ministry of the Interior there were problems all the time that Serb personnel complained about, his behaviour in terms of his own appointment and that of his associates. So there was already disunity in the MUP. There was bitterness, too, that not a single proposal could come through easily, whereas some could not come through at all, although it had been agreed upon previously what kind of distribution of posts should exist. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of the witness who came from Vogosca. If you remember what kind of appointment they wanted and that the municipality complained because they didn't want that appointment, and this Mandic, because he was in charge, went to the municipality to try to resolve the matter. So there was no unity in the MUP. On the contrary. The MUP was completely disunited for these reasons that went on and on throughout the year. I knew about this. I knew about that the dispatch had been sent, and I knew that Mr. Delimustafic later removed Mr. Mandic from office and that a document was sent to that effect. That was a day or two before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- you knew about Mr. Mandic's document in the way that you've described. You knew about Mr. Delimustafic's document as well, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found out about Mr. Mandic's document in Brussels. And as for this, I learned about it later. Now, was it in Brussels? Was it Sarajevo? I don't remember, but I knew about this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally take any steps whatever to speak to anybody or do anything yourself in relation to this issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although that was not within the scope of my authority, but since I was nearby, near the Executive Council building, Mr. Izetbegovic came to my office, and a man came from the government too. I think it was Mr. Pelivan, perhaps, the prime minister himself, but I'm not sure. And Mr. Delimustafic came. And I don't know who came from among the Serb appointees. We talked about the problem of the MUP which had culminated. We wanted to deal with these problems irrespective of the dispatch on which we all agreed. We all thought that it was not regular. But we discussed these problems, and Mr. Delimustafic was there at the time, and at one moment I even thought that he'd get a heart attack because he was so upset, because he was being criticised. They were saying that he was not taking timely action, and also that his associates were sabotaging his efforts. But this was just a meeting by way of consultations. It was a government problem, but we talked about it as people from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina because, of course, we wanted to avoid a crisis. It was a state affair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know at the time somebody called Bakir Alispahic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Mr. Alispahic directly. I know the family, though. They are from Ahatovici. Perhaps I know him directly too. That's in the area of Rajlovac. That's where his family hailed from. But I had no contact with him while he held this position in the MUP, or at least I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- did you know at the time whether he was in any way involved in this issue about Mr. Mandic's instruction and then Mr. Delimustafic's communication that we saw a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with any degree of certainty. I knew of the problem in general terms. At that time, perhaps I even knew the details, but now I cannot recall the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, just going back to that Law on Internal Affairs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could I just try to put one question so that -- to see whether I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I heard your testimony, and I understood the following, and please correct me when I'm wrong, because I'm really trying to understand as good as I can. The law was adopted. The law was promulgated. Then the constitution was promulgated as well, and then Mr. Mandic comes with a dispatch of which you say it was not correct because the government had not yet done what it should have done under Article 25 of that law, so therefore Mr. Mandic was not in a position nor were the formalities met which could lead to the implementation of that law. And then you have drawn our attention to a message sent by Mr. Delimustafic -- Delimustafic, in which he says that the MUP should be united, should not be split up. Forget about a dispatch. That's not something we -- you should obey. Now, I do understand that Mr. Delimustafic was minister of the MUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina, not the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It doesn't come to me as a surprise that where, I would say, the whole exercise of creating a new constitution, adopting new laws, et cetera, et cetera, was not something that had any support, in general terms, I would say, of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because it was a kind of -- well, parallel structure for Serbs. And then Mr. Delimustafic sends a message to the MUPs and says stay united. So he tries to undermine whatever effect this dispatch of Mr. Mandic would have had. Now, I can imagine that if you have two competing units, that one is the -- well, let's say, at that time the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, if this was considered to be illegal in the view of those responsible for the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would have expected that not only the -- I would say the other government would have criticised the dispatch but that the Republic of the Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina would also have taken distance, because I can imagine that in view of the relation between the one government and the other that Serbs might not that much be impressed by a message which says ignore what has been sent to you by Mr. Mandic, but that if you really want to take distance, that you would not leave it to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina but that the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina would also have clearly expressed its own view. Therefore, first of all, I'm seeking confirmation of whether I well understood your testimony, and I added to that a rather long question about what I would expect under those circumstances. Could you please, first of all, confirm that my understanding of your testimony was right, and then second, comment on what appears to me not immediately logical; that is, that only Delimustafic criticised it and not anyone from within the Serbian -- from the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judge is always right. I wish I could say you were right, but there are some small corrections that need to be made, and they are important. Mr. President, the constitution of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 28th of -- was not adopted on the 28th of February. It was not promulgated on the 28th of February. It was promulgated on the 27th of March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was a slip of -- yes, yes. It was between the publication of the Law on Internal Affairs and the dispatch of Mr. Mandic. Yes. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This promulgation of this law, you can see that the two acting appointees did what they did. They said, "We are promulgating this law. And even that was unlawful. Another thing that I wish to say why we did not refute this, because that is what you find the most important, Mr. Delimustafic first derogated Mr. Mandic's dispatch. In my statement I said that he did not have the right, according to the constitution or any other act, or according to the law, Mr. Mandic did not have the right to do that. That is one thing. Secondly, as for the leadership of Republika Srpska, why didn't they send the same kind of dispatch? I've already said, first of all, there wasn't enough time. And secondly, also we had already reached agreement on the MUP being within the jurisdiction of the Republic of the Serb People. And that is what our constitution says towards the end, that that constitution would fit into the results of the conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it is not an independent state. That was the core of the matter. We did not want to refute. Well, we didn't even have any time. We didn't want to do what Mr. Delimustafic did because we would have created a great deal of confusion. We wanted to resolve the actual causes which led to the chaos in the MUP on the ground. Mr. Mandic acted quite unconstitutionally. He did not have the powers to do this. However, this is the constitution of the 27th of March. It is only on the basis of this constitution that laws could be passed. All of this was done clumsily, if I could put it that way, and it was unfounded. So a great deal of effort had to be made in order to rectify all the mistakes. Now, what you are asking about and what is a sensitive issue is the following: The Serb side was not against the future solution of Bosnia-Herzegovina envisaging a MUP of its own, of the Serb side. On the contrary, we advocated that. But this was to be done through agreement by all three sides, and this agreement was indeed reached by all three sides. So it wasn't Mandic who he had the right -- who had the right to say that. It should have been the parliament or the government, but we didn't have a parliament or government. So with all due respect to the entire context, this is not just one problem. There are a lot of irregularities involved. We could not say no, we do not want a MUP of our own. No. On the contrary. We wanted the Republika Srpska to have a MUP of its own because that had been agreed upon. Now, we didn't have time. We had redressed the problems of the MUP, do you understand that, regarding appointments and everything else, all of this that led to this rift. There was very little time, because on the ground there were constant divisions on appointments. That was criticism. We were not dealing with this dispatch which was probably an effect of that but in an inappropriate way. I don't know if I managed to give you an explanation. Perhaps I complicated things even further, but this is a very complex matter, and I try to tell you about it in as pithy a way as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I now better understand. Judge Hanoteau also has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know if we agree on the fact that this law was published in the Official Gazette on the 23rd of March, 1992. Do we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Official Gazette was then sent throughout the country, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Maybe not. I will tell you, Your Honour. If you remember, there was a trial going on here, and Mr. Treanor testified, and he said that what they did was an improvisation because there were no documents on the ground. They had not been distributed. I don't know whether this one distributed or not. It might well not have been because the time was very short. And when it is published on the 23rd, it takes a couple of days to print it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, is this right: What you -- what you seem to be saying is that the -- the legal and constitutional arrangements at that time were got into some sort of tangle and that errors were made.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear you quite well, and it seems important. If you mean that it was very confused, that it was complicated by a hundred different interventions, then you're right. But I didn't hear all of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, I was putting it to you that what you have been saying, among other things, is that the legal and constitutional arrangements at that time for the Republika Srpska or the Serb republic were got into some sort of tangle and that errors were made.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way, although it was actually done deliberately that way. We wanted things done stage by stage, and we wanted to have the constitution proclaimed to have certain arguments and to send a message to the other side, "Look, we are taking this path and let us agree on this." That's why on the 25th or -- I don't know which date in February the constitution was passed, and we postponed its promulgation. It wouldn't have been promulgated even on the 27th had it not been for the fact that we were going to that conference, and they then made this statement that they wanted independence at all costs, and they were not going to negotiate about that. They will have a unitary state. And then we decided to do this, leaving a hand outstretched to them promulgating this constitution that was to be built into the constitution of Republika Srpska. It does look confused, as Mr. Stewart says, but certain laws were indeed adopted deliberately because of political needs, for political considerations. However, when a certain move is made without thinking it through very carefully, like this one was made, it can have very grave consequences. Let me just remind you that on the 24th of March, one MP from Pale, Veselinovic, or maybe it was the 18th of March, he told me at the Assembly, "We want to bring up the question of MUP at the Assembly session," and I told him, "Leave it until the 27th," because we were dealing with a lot of grave problems. The reserve force people getting armed. And that's why this story of Mr. Delimustafic was sham. It was sham when he said that there were no problems, that they were united, et cetera. Every day a new problem arose. Maybe not every day but almost.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The analysis which you offered a little while ago this afternoon based on looking at Article 25 together with Article 129 of the Law of Internal Affairs, is this, Mr. Krajisnik, an analysis which you have only done since you were brought to The Hague but never did before that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say you're right. But even during the war I was aware that nothing can be done. It's illogical, I know, but I had enough time here in The Hague, and I was able to analyse this and compare it all, especially after the testimony of Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The reason I say that, Mr. Krajisnik, and perhaps I'll say this for you and in effect with respect to the Trial Chamber and everybody else, is that I have not called you, and you have not been called for the Defence as an expert legal witness, Mr. Krajisnik. You are the defendant, and you are a witness of fact. So there are limits to what I wish to explore with you in the light of that answer. But if we look at -- nevertheless, at Article 126 again, and could you just -- could you have that in front you and focus on that for the purposes of this next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're being handed it again, Mr. Krajisnik. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, if -- if the government of the Serb republic, Republika Srpska, took no steps to implement Article 126, and if Mr. Mandic and any of his colleagues when he was within the government took no steps to implement this Article and no steps of the sort that Mr. Mandic didn't take, based on this Article 126, what would have happened on the day that this law came into effect, on the day that Article 126 said that the centres for public security services and public security stations of the MUP on the territory of the Serb people of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be closed? In real life, what would have happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a lawyer, and I didn't write this law, but I know what it looks like in practice. There was no government. No matter how many laws you had, they couldn't begin to be enforced without the enforcers, without the ministers, without the government, and without this and that. This was not put into practice because nobody obeyed this dispatch. Nobody complied with the dispatch written by Mr. Mandic in those two days. And later on, the war started. And when the war started, the situation changed completely. Unfortunately, we have an overlap between wars of force majure and this law that was supposed to come into force. Had it not been for the war, the government would have been established, the minister appointed. The minister would have approved this law and sent it to technical services. He would have appointed secretaries and assistants and then it would have started to function. You cannot do some thing without letters of appointment, without -- I don't know what. This was impracticable at that moment. It would have been practicable once you had a government and all the other prerequisites. The war brought with it a new set of facts, but the dispatch of Mr. Mandic didn't. The situation changed due to other forces and not this law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm moving to another topic now, so I see where the clock is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we are moving to another subject, perhaps we first will have the break. We'll have a break until ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I want to go to the 10th Assembly Session of the Serb Assembly, which was on the 11th of March. And, Your Honour, I believe that we are all going to be working from the same version of the English. It was exhibited as P65, binder 9A, tab 107.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to give you page references as we go along. You should in most cases have the familiar by now numbering as well. Can we go to page 4 of the English please, the foot of page 4. This should be on page 5 probably of the -- your version, Mr. Krajisnik, but it's got the margin number 1. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's 00816439, if I can help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very same, I think, Mr. Krajisnik. The paragraph begins: "Europe has --" it's Dr. Karadzic speaking. He says: "Europe has realised and accepted --" no, I better read the couple of sentences in the previous paragraph otherwise it doesn't make much sense. From the middle of the previous paragraph: "We have decided on a compromise," and he's talking it becomes quite clear about these Cutileiro discussions. "We have decide on a compromise to the effect that if the Muslim and Croat --"

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Is that before the 1?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's just before.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beg your pardon. Going back to the previous paragraph. "We have decided --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: We have not found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It's on page 4 and it's the -- about 20 lines up, the paragraph beginning "We have not pleaded for." And then it's in the middle of that paragraph, Your Honour. I can pick it up in the middle, "We have decided."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's my fault, Your Honour, I was going a bit quick there. "We have decided upon a compromise to the effect that if the Muslim and Croat ethnic communities do," and that "not" seems to be quite wrong, Mr. Krajisnik. It should read: "Ethnic communities do wish to leave Yugoslavia and the Serbian community does not wish to leave Yugoslavia, i.e., does not want to lose its state for that state is Yugoslavia, the whole BH could exist even then within the current borders. It could change its position vis-a-vis Yugoslavia, without the Serbian people changing their position, namely without falling under the domination of the majority people, that is the Muslim ethnic community, within the current BH borders. "Europe has realised and accepted this in part, and at the first meeting in Lisbon, we were already offered a document envisaging constituent states in BH, which were, in Izetbegovic's case, interpreted as constituent units rather than constituent states, set up on ethnic principles. The other side stated that this would also include economic, geographical and other criteria, which we find fully acceptable, because it is not our intention to create something meaningless in terms of economy and geography, something that does not guarantee viability." And, Mr. Krajisnik, there, and it may not be necessary for us to take time to go back to the documents at this point. But there Dr. Karadzic is referring, isn't he, to a change which was made between the two versions of the agreement or proposed agreement that we looked at the other day, the second version, which is D5 in our exhibits as opposed to D6, the second version introduced, didn't it, an extra element to the definition of territory of the constituent units to take into account economic, geographical and other criteria?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We could look at the documents, Mr. Krajisnik, but at the moment I'm not suggesting that we need to. The -- and that in -- that proposal came from the Muslims, but it was not resisted by your team of negotiators, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not resist. On the contrary. All the four sides agreed. That was a consensus on that. Between Muslims, Croats, Serbs, and the European Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic continues, and it's against point 2 in the margin of your copy. It's at the top of page 5 in English: "The talks in Sarajevo, after Lisbon, nevertheless ended in a fiasco, because Mr. Izetbegovic, having returned from Lisbon immediately tried to play down and devaluate had been achieved there." And, Mr. Krajisnik, was it the position that at the time that you were holding this Assembly meeting on the 11th of March there had been no further change of Mr. Izetbegovic's position? He was expressing himself rather negatively in relation to -- to this proposed agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a preliminary paper that the three sides had not agreed on yet, and you will see nobody either rejected or accepted it. It was still only a working paper. And the Serb side would later have reservations concerning this paper. Yes, that's the 11th Session -- sorry, the 11th, and on the 18th accepted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, then, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps we can look at -- we don't need look at both documents but if we could look again at D5. Now, you -- the document in front of you, you have this document in English there, do you, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have it in Serbian or maybe Croatian. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- the document -- this is the document which bears the date at the end, Sarajevo, 18 March, 1992, but at this point, 11th of March, when you were having the Assembly session, was the latest form of document that had emerged from the Cutileiro talks in the form of this draft which came to be in some way adopted or in some way approved on the 18th of March, or was it -- was the document in a different earlier state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you give me both the documents, I will tell you which version is the first and which is the second, because this is the second version that I'm holding now. On the first version, there are years, '71, '81 and '91. So this is the Sarajevo agreement, whereas the other one is the first version of the Lisbon Agreement that was discussed on this session on the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to worry about that. It's already from your evidence and general it's already been clearly established that the document that we have at D6 came before the document that you're looking at now. My question -- if you -- if you don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure if you -- it's still clear what question you're answering yes to, Mr. Krajisnik. My -- my question --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this is the second version, whereas the other one, D6, is in fact the first version that was on the table in Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. My question is this, Mr. Krajisnik: The latest version of the document as you had it at the time of this Assembly meeting on the 11th of March, was it changed the following week on the 18th of March or did the document, as far as you remember, remain in the same state?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of March, there were amendments and additions and corrections to the document that was discussed in Lisbon and that was also the subject of debate on the 11th of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the point 4A, which is at the top of page 7 in the English, and it's on page 8 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have it on page 7, 4A, if you said 4A, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter. If you've got 4A, Mr. Krajisnik. A paragraph that begins "Pursuant to item 2." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Pursuant to item 2, we are required to confirm that neither the governments nor the Assemblies of the national states will support or encourage any request for any part of their territories to be annexed to neighbouring states."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We never had any ambitions or ideas to join a part of BH to Serbia, but we had ambitions to exercise our rights to statehood and sovereignty here where we live." Is -- is that correct where Dr. Karadzic says, "We never had any ambitions or ideas to join a part of BH to Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Either the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina was to be a part of Yugoslavia or Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state was to be transformed. And we didn't ask in those negotiations for our part to be joined to Serbia. So this statement is completely accurate, and you can see that from all the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it accurate as a statement of your, the Bosnian Serbs, position in those Cutileiro negotiations but also as a statement of what your own private policy had been?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I have said here before that we were pursuing a realistic policy. We knew what was possibly. And we no longer dwelled on any private different opinions of ours. We took a realistic position that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be independent and we would have a constituent unit in it. We accepted that we wouldn't be in Yugoslavia. We accepted that there would be an independent Bosnia, and in exchange we would get a transformed Bosnia with three constituent nation-based units with all respect of all the cultural, economic, and other autonomy principles. That was the deal. It was a trade-off. They had to abandon the idea of their unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we had to give up the idea of being within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go to page -- well, it's page 11 of the -- page 15 of your version, page 11 of the English. It's actually over the page, page 16 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik. You've got a marginal number 6B, and it's the bottom paragraph on page 11 of the English. The paragraph beginning "During my stay there." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it. I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the context there is England in that case. "During my stay there I was invited to attend a debate on Yugoslavia --" sorry, I should have said it's Dr. Koljevic talking here. "I was invited to attend a debate on Yugoslavia in the British Parliament, and heard four very interesting things on which both the Conservatives and the representatives of the Labour Party insisted. I have a facsimile summary thereof which I got from journalists. For our orientation, this was a highly interesting presentation of our truths. And you know how poorly the Serbs performed in the media world and if it were not for that there would have been no demands on our part from TV Sarajevo which is not an independent television but a centre of power. The most interesting thing is that in the discussion they criticised the EC for the following," and then he goes on to certain matters. Mr. Krajisnik, was it -- from what you could see at that time, was it your view that the Serbs had performed poorly in the media world?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I was not involved in that area if I can put it that way. I was not involved in such issues. But I heard from people who know more about it, that the media promotion of Serb interests was at a low level and that we did perform poorly there. So I agree with what the late Mr. Koljevic says here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were your main spokespeople so far as the international community was concerned at this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were, each of them, very well equipped to conduct interviews in English, for example, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, when I said "spokesperson," I meant them because they could address the public in English, but we did not have a particular person who was at a lower level and who would speak on behalf of all of us. Perhaps from time to time there would be someone, but for the most part it was the two of them who spoke. Well, they were not exactly people who played the role of a spokesperson, so that's why I said they presented our views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you speak, Mr. Krajisnik, at page 19 of your version, the very foot of page 13 of the English. "Chairman: Thank you, Mr. Koljevic." And then it says -- well it says: "Mr. Krajisnik has the floor." But you were the chairman, Mr. Krajisnik, weren't you, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say at the top of page 14 of the English, at the beginning of that: "I shall not try to repeat what my predecessors have said," and so on. And then the next paragraph: "Lest I, perhaps, forget at the end, I would like to suggest something imputed by the EC: Namely, that the three of us," and the three of you -- the three negotiators meant you, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic and you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The three of us would try to talk you into not accepting this document, but rather that this session of the Assembly is being held to explain how it should not be done. That is why I would like to ask you not to allow the discussion to be conducted as if the three of us were intimating this was something damaging for the Serbian people but rather with the aim of determining what is to the benefit or in the interest of the Serbian people, and what is not to the detriment of others." In saying, Mr. Krajisnik, that it had been imputed by the EC, are you able to say who specifically in the course of those talks had suggested that the three of you would try to dissuade the Serb Assembly from accepting the document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this paper that was here, this Assembly, was more or less fully unacceptable for all three sides. Our side had some reservations, too, because there had been a change in the position compared to what we had agreed upon previously. When this paper was finalised, if I can put it that way, then someone, I don't know who, that's my answer, I don't know who, I cannot say whether it was Mr. Cutileiro, but -- well, you see, we were not negotiating directly. We were in three different rooms and then he walked around. It was a kind of shuttle diplomacy. Then it was imputed to us that it was not true that the Assembly disagreed with this but that we would explain to the Assembly that something said here was wrong. And then I asked the chairman to chair the Assembly session while I spoke so that this would not be -- and then I asked him to chair the entire session so that they would not impute to me that I was doing something that was not right. This was a good foundation. The paper just needed a bit more work. But for the MPs, this was a turnaround. They expected a great deal more, but mercifully the conclusion was a positive one ultimately, but it could have been rejected outright. Perhaps I could say that it was Mr. Cutileiro, but well, I don't know. I don't know who it was. But this objection was voiced to us that we would now be against it because there were changes as compared to the talks that we had had previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. My apologies. I think I had missed the fact that you had had handed over the chair to Mr. Milanovic at some point earlier in the meeting, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, I didn't notice that. It is Professor Dr. Milan Milovanovic, vice-president of the Assembly. There were two vice-presidents. He was the one who chaired the Assembly meeting at this point. I think that he chaired the meeting later, too, so that the president of the Assembly could not influence the MPs in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we see that at page 9 the English. I think Mr. Milovanovic not only mispronounced by me but lost a syllable in his name as well, but that's where it happens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- at where we -- we --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name is Milanovic, Milanovic, but there is also a person called Milovanovic, but the vice-president is Milovan Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at page -- now page 20, please, of your version. This is page 14 of the English. And it's you still speaking. You say: "Another point I wish to make is that if we cannot find a common arrangement for joint life, then this people and this Assembly must be asked whether they accept something contrary to the will of the people, the will of the people explicitly voiced at the plebiscite. I think that none of the possibilities underlying our policy and the policy upheld by the Serbian people has been exhausted, but that is own -- it is only necessary to choose the most realistic one at the given moment, the one most adjustable to the times. And despite the fact that I might be misunderstood by some, I personally cannot give up on the idea of the Serbian people living in one state or accept that Yugoslavia is an exhausted option irrespective of the fact that these two things should be given careful consideration." Mr. Krajisnik, what you say there about not giving up on the idea of the Serbian people living in one state or that Yugoslavia is an exhausted option, was that public politics you were adopting there, or was it genuinely your private view that you still retained some hope that one or -- of those matters might be brought about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for having put this question. We are presenting a concept which is contrary to the decision of the plebiscite of the Serb people; namely, to remain in Yugoslavia. I am saying that I personally can never give up on that, that all of us live in Yugoslavia together, all Serbs, all Croats, all Muslims. Here I was talking only about Serbs. But then I said we have to decide whether we want to pursue a realistic policy, or are we going to go on discussing something which at this point in time shows that the position of the international community is different. At that time, every Serb, including me, wanted Bosnia to be with Yugoslavia, but if we have this realistic option that Bosnia will be Bosnia, then we -- well, actually we worked in Lisbon on an option that was contrary to the plebiscite. So this entire discussion is, well, along the lines of yes, perhaps we all agree on this, but we have to look at the actual balance of power, and that is the meaning of my words. If Serbs were to be interviewed today, whether they wanted live this way or that way, the result would probably be the same. But many things are based on a compromise. You do not resolve your problems on your own. It depends on others too. So that's the point. You can see that on the basis of what I said briefly and what I said later. Your Honours, I'm sorry, but I just need a bit more time. We were being told all the time what is this? At the plebiscite we said that we are in favour of Yugoslavia. Who was it that betrayed us? Why are we not staying in Yugoslavia? What kind of Bosnia is this now? And then of course you say, well, this is a reality. And as for what you're saying, yes, that is the view that was expressed, but then other things changed. This was an expression of views to see what people's positions were, but this was not a final decision. It would be as if somebody was bargaining with themselves and then if you have two other people who have an interest involved in that particular matter. So there was this bitter fight with the MPs so that they understand that the situation changed. To this day, some people have not forgiven us. They cannot understand why we gave up on Yugoslavia. We didn't give up. That's what the situation was. And people cannot understand that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm not always the best person to give this advice. I guess from the speed at which the interpreters are needing to go that it would be in your interest to slow down a bit. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thank you. I thank you all if you caution me this way. I don't understand that as an objection. I know it's really difficult when people speak this fast. It's a question of temperament. I speak that way. But anyway, whoever cautions me, the only thing I can do is say thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik, you say: "Allow me, thanking again. Allow me to thank you for the confidence placed in me by the Serbian people and you ladies and gentlemen deputies both in the Assembly and as a representative of the Serbian people to this delegation. I think that it would be rational, useful and good to refresh the negotiating team. I suggest that someone among those present here be nominated to replace me so that something new might be introduced, because it is evident that certain things must be adjusted to the situation we have found ourselves in. I would recommend that it be a jurist or another professor, a member of the Presidency. I will not nominate anyone now." Mr. Krajisnik, whose idea was it that you would make this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was imputed that Momcilo Krajisnik was powerful because these negotiations were one of our most important tasks. And at the club of deputies, there were several people who wanted to be on that delegation because they thought they would handle it better or they wanted to be important or whatever. You are not doing your best for the option of Yugoslavia. Something else would be better. Why did you give this territory? And so on and so forth. Quite simply - how should I put this - the people who were there did not understand why the whole model was being changed. Then I said what I said previously. Well, perhaps I would have liked that just like you, but I don't have the right not to pursue a realistic policy. So they did not raise these objections vis-a-vis me but vis-a-vis all three of us. I said, well, it's not about me. Choose whoever you want except for me. Let me just digress a bit. On the 25th of July, I made the same proposal and a few other times, because I did not want to be the subject of this discussion as to whether I could do more or not. And all negotiations are difficult when people work on that. After the club of deputies, well, this came from the government and from Mrs. Plavsic and so on, and I said, well, propose whoever you want. Just replace me. Especially because I had personal problems of my own, family problems that I've already emphasised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then a little -- well, two paragraphs further on. That will be at page 21 of your document, Mr. Krajisnik, at the top of page 15 of the English, or nearly at the top. The paragraph beginning: "The third thing I wanted to ask you is to bear in mind in today's debate that there is a very serious problem, namely that it is not only the interests of our two partners which are opposed to us but that objectively a much greater power than these two sides is opposed to us, notably the interests of Europe." Where did you see the main conflict between the interests of Europe and the interest of you, the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Europe, and when I say "Europe" it was the European Community that was the mediator, when they come, then the Muslims say one thing, the Croats say another thing, and the Serbs say yet a third thing, and it's not possible to find a solution. So then we try to reach a compromise. Nobody likes that compromise very much but the representatives of Europe say we are not going to support you in your maximalist interests. And that was Yugoslavia. We are not going to support you in having a unitary Bosnia, and so on and so forth. Now, what am I saying? You have to understand that the objective of Europe is to find a solution. Now, they shaped their proposal on the basis of our interests. Well, our proposals. So, yes, we have the Muslims and the Croats against us, but we also have Europe there too. We could hardly wait for Europe to come because we could not reach an agreement amongst ourselves, and that was true. And then I pointed out that there were four sides, because if somebody came to help, he's not going to side with one side only, of course. Perhaps I'm not putting this very nicely if I say interest, but then there is a proposal. There is a position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, we can perhaps just note that it's at the foot of page 15 of the English that Mr. Koljevic makes a short contribution, and he does support your proposal that you should stand down and be replaced as a member of the negotiating team, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. Mr. Koljevic is saying here that he supports me, and I think that it would have to say here that he said that he was prepared to see other people brought in, and he includes himself there, because it wasn't I who was criticised. The delegation was criticised. Perhaps you'd like me to read this. Perhaps the team should be refreshed, in a way, and you will see later that he is suggesting that even he should be replaced, because before that people criticised us saying that our delegation had not done very much and could have done much more. I'm not sure whether that is what it says here or -- but, anyway, he supports me here in terms of these changes in the delegation or this refreshment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any suggestion --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Of course we think that the head of the delegation must remain, but then new results might be obtained by introducing new players into the game. Well, that's what he's saying. This is how this should be understood. Change the two of us and find somebody. Sorry for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did anyone ever suggest that Dr. Karadzic might cease to be the leader of the negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have pointed out that there were objections vis-a-vis the delegation. Mr. Koljevic put this very well. If the three of us are the delegation, then, he says, it would be a good thing if the head of the delegation were to remain. And I support Krajisnik in terms of refreshing the delegation, and, of course, if it's the two of us, then replace one of the two of us. Then since I had proposed that I should be replaced -- well, I wasn't talking about him. I didn't propose a replacement for Karadzic. No one made any proposals to the effect that Mr. Karadzic should be replaced. On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, could you go on then, please, to page 42, which is page 28 of the English.
