And it's -- it's towards the end of a contribution by Mr. Buha, Aleksa Buha. And he says about -- just going a little way up from where you see the 8C in the margin. There are a couple of bullet points or points with dashes, and he says: "I believe that we should insist on the following." Do you see that introduction? It's about three or four paragraphs from the end of his contribution.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, but the beginning is probably different. Could you just give me the actual sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. "I believe that we should insist on the following," and then it goes down a couple of lines, " - this shy quasi-language must be abandoned ..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: " ... must be abandoned and things called by their real names. "The first real name to be expressed is that this Bosnia and Herzegovina in its present borders can only be a union of independent ethnic republics of the Serbian, Croatian and Muslim peoples. "When this option is formulated, and I think the document contains elements for something along these lines, things will take a much easier and more favourable turn for all the three peoples in BH. "We should therefore insist that as far as the Serbian people in BH is concerned there can exist only independent ethnic republics, individually, and at the level of the entire BH, a union of independent republics or states, ethnic ones, in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So just to invite you to make it clear, Mr. Krajisnik, was this to be understood as Dr. -- Mr. Buha opposing what was under consideration in the Cutileiro talks and wishing to go for a stronger position that this should be a fully sovereign, independent Serb republic carved out of the Bosnia and Herzegovina territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Buha was a member of the delegation. He must have been a member of the delegation here as well. He was trying to sell his model to the MPs. He's trying here to exaggerate the complexity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he is painting this alliance of independent states a bit thick. There's no longer any talk of Yugoslavia. There's only talk about Bosnia and Herzegovina. The discussion continued, never ceased whether it would be a federation or a union or whatever. I just want to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to this: The Dayton Accords refer only to Bosnia and Herzegovina. It doesn't specify in the Dayton Accords whether it's a union or a federation or a republic, because we couldn't agree what to call it. It just says Bosnia and Herzegovina. So that later during the negotiations we came to the union of three republics, et cetera, et cetera. This complexity, we didn't want to separate it from what we had earlier agreed. Whatever we call it, it has to be one Bosnia and Herzegovina and one chair in the United Nations. That was beyond debate. That was indisputable. So when Mr. Buha was saying this, mentioning this alliance and the confederation, that, too, would be one entity in the United Nations. Of course, even this contribution of his, acceptable as it is, was not endorsed by the deputies because the deputies kept thinking that things could be much better still. They couldn't get over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what do you say the deputies would have understood Mr. Buha to be saying by the use of the word "independent" in the phrase "independent ethnic republics"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the terminology that prevailed in our former system, we used the term "internal independence," "external independence," "independence transferred powers," et cetera, et cetera. Mr. Buha was a wise man. He's playing up to the deputies by using terms pleasing to their ears. He's saying, "We will define what Bosnia will be, because a state is a state, and the complex state union is a complex thing." And even this is remote from the idea, the concept, and even that was not acceptable. The time wasn't ripe. In six -- six, seven days later, things changed completely. Although it may seem that way, Mr. Buha never advocated anything unrealistic in terms of policy, although very often during negotiations in order to obtain an optimal solution we said we will ask for independence, et cetera. We were pulling the rope to our side in that tug-of-war, because you have to start with -- with the more maximalist option so that the eventual compromise doesn't water down your -- your original objective too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Krajisnik, the -- the deputies at this Assembly, they had copies of the latest form of the document under discussion in the Cutileiro talks in front of them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid there might be a misunderstanding. They had the first version from Lisbon. They didn't have the Sarajevo agreement. The Sarajevo agreement was the final version, after we agreed. If I remember correctly, it's 6B here. It came -- or, rather, the version that was discussed by the MPs at that moment came before the Sarajevo agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the misunderstanding I'm afraid of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's always possible that something creeps in in the interpretation. When I put it to you that you had copies of the latest form of the document, that was intended to convey the latest that was in existence at the time of this meeting and not the ultimate last one that lay in the future but the most up-to-date version of the document is what they had; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's -- that's all right. We're on the same wavelength now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And the reason I was suggesting that just for the reference is it's apparent in bits of this transcript that we went over that there's quite detailed reference by Dr. Karadzic, isn't there, to provisions of the document which would have been incomprehensible to anybody who didn't have it in front of them. Mr. Krajisnik, it's -- the reference is to around page 7 in the English. I think we can move on safely from there. We get Mr. Nikola Perisin. I think we've seen him before. He picks up at the bottom of page 28 in the English, and that will be probably page 43 or so of the Serbian. But I want to move on a bit in his contribution a couple of pages to -- it would be page 45, possibly at the foot of page 44 of the Serbian, and it's at page 30 of the English. And he says -- there's a paragraph beginning: "We have absolute Croatian rule in Brod." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "This is occupation by a foreign state, a foreign army, to which we are regrettably not reacting with sufficient arguments and clarity, not to mention the legal organs of the still legitimate authorities of BH. This is a taking of our pulse and a test of patience. The next phase is certainly the area of Posavina, i.e., the taking of positions in Derventa, Modrica after which they will have only a very small number of unoccupied territories, for instance Rudan near Doboj. They have publicly stated this to be their objective. I expect that if we really patiently and passively watch what is taking place that they will occupy their territory in the next 10 to 15 days. There is no more dilemma in that respect. In addition to their political activities, they have really manifested their intentions in the purely military domain." Mr. Krajisnik, when Mr. Perisin was saying he expected that they will occupy their territory in the next 10 to 15 days, who did you understand he was saying would occupy what territory? Was it -- what -- was it -- no, I'll leave it in that bare form. Who was going to occupy what territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about Nikola Perisic, not Perisin. Perisin is a mistake. But let me explain -- although it does say "Perisin" in the original, but I know exactly who this person is. He was the president of a municipality, and I believe he held some other post as well. Let me explain what these questions mean. Regardless of Serb territories in Posavina, Croats were saying that the entire Posavina belonged to them. Modrica, Derventa, and all the rest. And when he says that he would take all their territories, he means those territories that they are drawing for themselves in their own map. Perisic is not protesting against them taking ethnic Croat areas, because Croats were not alone in the population of Brod. I even believe Serbs were a majority, and the same is true of Modrica and Derventa. The underlying meaning of all his contribution is that regular Croat forces helped install a fully Croat government in Brod, although it was supposed to be divided between the three sides. And if you remember this conversation between Mr. Koljevic and me when he says I had been to Slavonski Brod on the other side of the Sava River, this ties in with that conversation. Later there were conflicts and visits from -- visits by the delegation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's part of their territory. It's what they consider to be their territory. It has a historical dimension as well. It used to be a part of the Croatian banovina, and even though the situation had changed, the Croats wanted all of Posavina to be Croat territory without any regard to any other people who may populate it. That's the meaning of what Mr. Perisic was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you -- you mentioned in that answer that you believe that the Serbs were a majority in Brod and the same was true of Modrica and Derventa. On the map, P211, that large coloured map that we looked at the other day, it's -- Bosanski Brod is shown with a relative Croat majority, 41 per cent; Serbs, 34 per cent. Since that is the information on the map based on the 1991 census, it doesn't take you particularly by surprise to find that your supposition that the Serbs were in a majority is in fact wrong, does it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm wrong. I just said it like that because I know there is a certain part of Serb territories. But just like you are wrong in looking constantly on that map, just as Mr. Okun did, when the map is completely wrong for the purposes of our discussion. You should look at the other map that is divided into smaller areas, that shows municipalities. It was the other map that was the basis for our discussions, whereas this map that you are holding only created confusion. However, as far as percentages are concerned, you are completely right. I don't really have the figures in my head. Nobody had absolute majority, and I take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that there's -- that it's a mistake where it say -- where you said, Mr. Krajisnik, you should look at the other map that is divided into smaller areas that shows municipalities. I take it that you wanted to refer to smaller entities than municipalities, like local communes, or at least divided up more precisely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, you are right. Smaller parts of municipalities, like communes, et cetera. The one that Mr. Stewart is holding shows municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm holding several at the moment, Your Honour. The one that Mr. Krajisnik was mentioning a moment ago and which Your Honour just corrected that particular point about the terminology is P293. It's somewhere else as well but it's P293.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I should just mention that the map P211, the one that you didn't like a moment ago, it does confirm and we see that -- that the Serbs were in the majority in the other two municipalities mentioned, Derventa and Modrica. That's clear on the figures. So, Mr. Perisic here, he's said to the meeting what he "predicts or expects will happen if we really patiently and passively watch." And he says: "And what have we been doing? Truth to tell, we are relying on the army. We have endorsed such support here, and it is clear to me that we are relying on the army, which, frankly speaking, is absolutely not a reliable support. We are relying on an army which has been absolutely beheaded in ideological terms, an army without a state, an army which is in my opinion, and regrettably, trying to come out of this difficult situation in BH intact and with the clearest and best possible personal positions. An army declaring itself a neutral force which will separate the conflicting sides. It is clear that we can do nothing but rely on the army." Mr. Krajisnik, how nearly or otherwise would you at that time have supported the views being put forward there by Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The truth lies somewhere in between Mr. Perisic's opinion and mine. I was almost in love with the army. I -- I like the military profession as a vocation. And at that time, many people saw the army as communists and totally unprepared, although in fact the army was in a difficult position. It was equidistant from the sides involved and from the parties involved, and I thought that was perfectly all right. So if there was any truth in assertions that there was no strong entity behind the state, behind the army, no state behind it, no command in Belgrade, it is also true that the army was in trouble because conscripts were not answering call-ups, and there were many other problems. Mr. Perisic did not go into the deeper reasons for those problems in the army. He just criticised the army. He's saying we have no other army. We have no paramilitary formations. And the army that we have is weak, so what are we relying on in fact?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Perisic, from right up in the north of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the border with Croatia, his concerns being expressed here specifically relate to Croats, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's from Teslic originally. But he spoke about that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand all that he was saying here? Did he understand it to relate only to issues between Serbs and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood him to be talking about Posavina, only about problems between Croats and Serbs as far as Posavina is concerned. And as for the Yugoslav People's Army, it's a completely different issue. You probably meant this former issue. Because in Posavina, the overall population was more or less evenly divided, or there were more Croats. I think most of these municipalities had a Croat majority. In some municipalities they may even have had absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he continues by saying, "We have no parallel formations," a point which you just alluded to a moment ago, Mr. Krajisnik. Then he says, "At every meeting and talks with the army, our position was that we would disarm paramilitary formations if any appeared apart from the army. We have, regrettably, done so." But, Mr. Krajisnik, did you know anything about such meetings and talks with the army as were being referred to there by Mr. Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no, I don't know anything about it. But I'm afraid that you may be interpreting this not quite correctly. Mr. Perisic says, "We have no paramilitary formations." And then he says, "In our talks with the army," and I'm interpreting this now, "the army stated that it was against all paramilitary units and would disarm them all." And then he goes on to say that's why we don't have any. All of our men are in the army. That is the meaning of his contribution. When he said this, he meant that the Yugoslav People's Army would disarm all paramilitary units. They did not allow Serbs to have any paramilitary units, and we can hardly rely on the Yugoslav People's Army. That is the actual meaning of what he said here, and I'm afraid it can easily lend itself to misinterpretation. And they had on their territory various units, barracks, corps. They must have had some talks. Everybody held talks on the local level. When I say "everybody," I don't know really, but such contacts did take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I notice that you were reading a line as "we have no parallel formations," whereas Mr. Krajisnik quoted Mr. Perisic as saying, "We have no paramilitary formations." Could we please -- I haven't got the B/C/S in front of me. Could we just clarify what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That would be a good idea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see the paragraph? It's the previous paragraph that ends, and we needn't go there again. The previous paragraph ends: "It is clear that we can do nothing but rely on the army." You see that sentence, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please then just read out loud from the beginning of the immediately following paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We have no parallel formations. And at every meeting we had --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's already. The word seems to be, even from what I understood in the B/C/S, being "parallel" and not "paramilitary." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I must say it was a pretty fair speculation on Your Honour's part, but we got the answer anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, had you been involved by this time, it's the 11th of March, had you personally been involved in any discussions at all anywhere concerning the -- any difficulties relating to paramilitary formations, any questions of disarming paramilitaries, any issues about absorbing them into the regular army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you about what I know. I didn't take part in that. What I know is that the Supreme Command of the Yugoslav People's Army, on several occasions issued orders through General Kadijevic to disarm all paramilitary units starting with Croatia and continuing. I mean, starting from Croatia mostly, the war, there. But as for the disarming of any paramilitary formations, I didn't discuss that with anybody. I told you what meetings I had. That was on the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina with members of the General Staff of the JNA. And once, I think, I had a semi-private meeting with Mr. Kukanjac because he was speaking with the leaders in Sarajevo, but we didn't discuss those issues. Instead, he wanted to hear what we thought about how they could help prevent a conflict. And I think he escorted me to my home once when there was a conflict, a clash in Kupres, but I don't remember that I ever talked about this issue. But it's quite understandable, generally speaking, that the army was against paramilitary units. And later, the Serb army was against all parallel structures. In their eyes, anything parallel to and outside of the army was irregular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. We need some time for a few procedural matters, but I take it that they can be dealt with in ten minutes. So if you'd keep that in the back of your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, up to this -- we're still at 11th of March, this Assembly session. Up to that point had any of the Bosnian Serb leadership to your knowledge or in your hearing expressed any concerns about the activities of paramilitaries in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the sessions of the Assembly and you look at what Mr. Stanisic said and what the representatives of the MUP said when they expressed their concern over the arming of paramilitaries on the other sides, that is to say, the Patriotic League and the Croat side. I'm saying that information was coming in. I testified about that, that we received information of that kind. Once, I think it was on the 24th of March, Mr. Mica Stanisic said something about that. That is to say, that we had information about paramilitary formations going public on the other sides. As for the Serb side, our position was that we should seek protection with the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mentioned concerns about Patriotic League and the Croat side and then going forward to the 24th of March, but as at the 11th of March, then, had any of the Bosnian Serb leadership expressed concerns about the activities of Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not remember information to that effect. I was not aware of any paramilitary units in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I knew about volunteers who went to the Croatian theatre of war, but paramilitary formations being active within Bosnia-Herzegovina and among the Serb people, I really did not know of any such thing, and I don't think that any such thing existed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Perisic continues, and if we go, please, to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask for one clarification? Mr. Krajisnik, if you're saying "volunteers," do I understand correctly that you refer to volunteers as being members of regular army units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes, that's what I men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Perisic -- if you go to page 47 on your copy. I think the number may be very indistinct on the page, but page 47 and then 9A in the margin. It's in the middle of page 31, or just below page 31 in the English, Your Honours. He says, "I wanted to say this because perhaps this Assembly is not aware of the actual state of affairs. It is, believe me, on the verge of being unbearable. We had a seven-hour meeting of the Crisis Staff yesterday, and our principal task was to calm down the people, to tell the people from Ozren, Posavina, to wait, that perhaps the time had not come. And each day they see that village after village, position after position, is being lost." He's talking distinctly there, is he, Mr. Krajisnik, about continuing armed conflict in his area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the continuation of this discussion has to do with Posavina. If you remember on the map near Ozren there is this blue enclave. I showed that. They called it a mountain of sorts, and it was split up into five municipalities. That's the map that's better, if I can put it that way, than the other one. So that's at -- that's near Posavina. It borders on Posavina. Now he's saying I'm trying to pacify people. I'm telling them to calm down, and they see these paramilitary units taking up military positions in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we -- can we have the map that you regard as better, Mr. Krajisnik, P293? Perhaps it would be most convenient to have it on the ELMO. Could you point out then, Mr. Krajisnik, what you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: People of Ozren, that's what he says. This is the area of Ozren. And he says -- well, you see this. This is the area of Modrica and part of Derventa. The blue line here is part of Brod. And then this up here is order of Odzak. That's why I'm saying that the area can be seen much better here. The Croat side thought that all of this that used to be the banovina should be the Croatian side. When I was saying about what they considered to be their territory, this is the area where there's about 100.000 Serbs, and it's split up into several municipalities, five or six, I think. That's why I said that you could see better here, because in every one of these municipalities somebody can be a majority, because the municipality is viewed as a whole rather than this smaller part. There are other areas, too, where Serbs are a minority in a municipality and the municipality is Croat or Serb. Now, that is what I wanted to explain. And that can be seen very well here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as Mr. Perisic's area was concerned, Mr. Krajisnik, can you say, had there been -- had there been more or less continuous fighting there since the end of 1991 up to this time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, by way of illustration, Derventa and Modrica, for instance -- well, perhaps I'll exaggerate a bit now, were twice in Serb hands and twice in Croat hands. Or I don't know how it was. When he said people from Ozren and from Posavina, he was referring to this, when he's talking about these people where the Serbs territories are. So these are the people of Posavina where the Serbs are, and these are the people of Ozren.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- did the SDS leadership become or had -- over that period, since the end of 1991, had the SDS leadership become in any way actively involved in those continuing issues of conflict in Mr. Perisic's area?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it did not become involved. I've already explained. We were supposed to rely on the Yugoslav People's Army. But in addition to this that can be seen here, everyone was concerned, was worried in their own municipalities. Well, maybe they had weapons, too, but I don't know about that. They were worried about their own mini location. Now, will somebody from Posavina take the Serb ethnic areas. From the Serb point of view, that is what people thought. I don't know what the other side was thinking. It was probably along similar lines but just the other way around. This is the Serb point of view, and that is how I interpret it. But the Serb Democratic Party, apart from political support to stimulate mobilisation, did not carry out any other activities. I don't know of any, and I don't think that there were any. That can be analysed. On several occasions that was confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when Mr. Perisic referred to a seven-hour meeting of the Crisis Staff, had you known that there was a Crisis Staff there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know, but I assure you -- well, I've already explained this. To establish a Crisis Staff was just like saying good morning. If the situation was difficult, that is what people did at their own initiative. Quite certainly there was no need on any side. This is not to say that this was not encouraged by someone, that if somebody was in a crisis they would establish a Crisis Staff. People would get together and they'd elect some kind of leadership, and then they would see what they would do. Well, this is part of our legacy, and in every crisis that's what people would do. He mentions this Crisis Staff here, but anybody could have mentioned it, and I wouldn't have reacted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Perisic continues, and it's in the middle of the penultimate paragraph on page 31 of the English, page 47 of the Serbian, he continues: "If we sit by and watch that, I frankly tell you I dare no longer engage such politics. I am afraid, not so much of those who are my enemies, but of what I will tell my own people, and what we will say if tomorrow we find we have lost everything without having lifted a finger, without having put up any resistance. "If you are taking my words seriously, then I suggest that you sit down with the command of the Second Army District and simply make it clear to them: They can keep publicly proclaiming their neutrality, but let them do what others are doing in the field. Let them get out of the barracks, take strategic positions, relocate the weaponry. Let them distribute arms to the people. Members of 70 per cent of the units still have their weapons somewhere far away in the barracks. This is senseless and absolutely incomprehensible for me." Mr. Krajisnik, the Second Army District you've referred to, that included Sarajevo, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Second Army District included Sarajevo and all of Bosnia, and before that even part of Croatia, and Posavina and part of Knin. So was not only for Bosnia. In response to your question, yes, it did include Sarajevo, and that is where their headquarters were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General Kukanjac, whom you've mentioned on a number of occasions, he was in command there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He was commander. I don't know who was commander before him, and I don't know when he came. I can't remember, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had -- at the time of that Mr. Perisic was speaking here, had any request been made by the SDS leadership to General Kukanjac that his men should get out of the barracks, take strategic positions, relocate weaponry or distribute arms?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know and remember, there was no such order and no such thing was said. We did address the Assembly once saying that the Yugoslav People's Army should protect the Serb people. Now, in what period of time this was, I cannot remember. But as for these words, that we sent that, it was not taken in a compulsory sense. It was sort of an expression of panic and it never crossed anybody's mind to dictate to the Yugoslav People's Army what they would do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in fact if we go on just -- he says a few more things, Mr. Perisic. But then you speak, Mr. Krajisnik. That's page 32 of the English, and it's 49 in your copy, Mr. Krajisnik. President Momcilo Krajisnik: "I think that some clarification would be in order: We should not depart from the agenda. It was useful to hear about the major problems on the ground, but without any intention or criticising we must stick to the agenda and hear what is related to the relevant subject matter. "I kindly ask that we do not expand the subject. And it would not be good to have the army on the agenda now." Mr. Krajisnik, it wasn't on the agenda as you made clear to start with, but did you have any particular reason for resisting adding army discussion to the business of this Assembly session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not chairing the session, although it looks that way because it says "Chairman, Momcilo Krajisnik." I was sitting next to the vice-president who was chairing the session, so then I probably asked for the floor from that particular spot where three people sit. What I'm trying to say is there is an agenda. That was the plan. And then people want to talk and talk, and then they say things that were not on the agenda. That happened often that people would digress from the agenda and discuss matters that were also important, but that was supposed to be an item on the agenda of another session, or somebody should have asked for it to be included in the agenda at the very beginning of the meeting. We just complained to each other the way Mr. Perisic put it or something like that, but we could not adopt any binding conclusions on the Yugoslav People's Army. That is why I kept saying that we should stick to the agenda, because this was not on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it -- was it in any way an uncomfortable or awkward issue that the leadership would not have wished to be raised at this point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what kind of issue it would take for the leadership to be unwilling to discuss it. I don't see any reason not to discuss an issue at an Assembly session. It's just that we needed to have an agenda and to stick to it. I don't remember that there was a single item or an issue that we didn't want to discuss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the next speaker is -- is -- well, actually, the next speaker is a Mr. Mijatovic, but I -- with no disrespect to him I was then going to Ms. Plavsic, the middle of page 33 of the English. It's point 11 in the margin at page 50, Mr. Krajisnik. And she says: "I think we should adopt the remarks of Mr. Aleksa Buha, namely to have the term 'confederation of states' be incorporated into the material at any cost. Everything else should be derived therefrom." Now, as a matter of fact, the passage we looked at, Dr. -- Professor Buha, I think he is, which is at page 42 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, and at pages 26 to 28, the particular passage being at 28 as it is at page 42 of yours, in the English I can't find a reference to "confederation of states" in Mr. Buha's contribution, but, nevertheless, Mr. Krajisnik, the question arises. Mrs. Plavsic was making it clear here that she was supporting Mr. Buha, and she refers to expressly to "confederation of states." Is it correct that what you have used the term "confederation," you personally in the course of this evidence, you have used it to mean a confederation of states that would be internationally recognised, each of them, as separate sovereign states?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "alliance of states" here in the original, and that's what Mr. Buha said in his prior contribution. Mr. Buha made representations in order to make this project attractive to the deputies. And then Mrs. Plavsic says, "We need to introduce the term 'alliance of states.'" It can also be interpreted as "union of states." I don't know what Mrs. Plavsic exactly meant. Did she mean a union or alliance of independent states? But Mr. Buha certainly didn't mean it to be a union of internationally recognised states. He spoken instead of Bosnia and Herzegovina that should be called a union of Bosnian states, in the same sense as we say United States of America. But it was never the intention for this union of Bosnian states to have constituent units that would be internationally recognised. Only Bosnia and Herzegovina would be an internationally recognised subject. When I said "union," I used the term that we -- or, rather, when I spoke of the confederation of states, I was talking about the term that we used in our discussions, but Mr. Buha here spoke about the union of states. Mrs. Plavsic is a bit more radical. She goes a bit further, but even she did not mean that we should ask for an internationally recognised Serbian Republic. Maybe in August she defended that position, but here she just meant that it would be a union of entities, a union of states rather than the unitary state we were so afraid of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, Mr. Krajisnik started his answer by saying that it should read "alliance of states" rather than anything else. Could you please ask him to read the word and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, what I've just been trying to do is -- we've been, as quickly as we can, seeing if we can check which word was used by Mr. Buha, which word used by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on the English -- in the English on page 28, that might be a clue, although it might not clarify the issue really, because it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've just had the information, Your Honour, just even as we've just been speaking, from Mr. Sladojevic, that the words in the last paragraph at page 28 in the English, obviously I'm giving the page in the English, but the word used in Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. Always, Mr. Stewart, you know how I appreciate the assistance of our interpreters, so if there is one word which would need perhaps to correct then the translation, I would invite Mr. Sladojevic to read that word and then have the translation by our interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's what I was going to do. Your Honour, in fact, I wasn't even going to do that. What I was going to say, Your Honour, was we've established it is the same word in each place in Serbian, and we were going to stop there in accordance with Your Honour's guidelines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, we can, then having mentioned that, we could then of course in accordance with those guidelines hand it over to the interpreters. So it's the last sentence apart from the "thank you," it's the last sentence at page 42 of the Serbian just before Mr. Milanovic, I hope that is what he's called, speaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the other one is the first paragraph, short paragraph, in what Mrs. Plavsic says at page 50 of the Serbian. Those are the two passages, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that would be -- in English that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. In English it's 28, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Middle of 28 and the middle of 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's more or less exactly in the middle on each of those two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that word would be, Mr. Sladojevic, if it's the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He better say it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Union of states."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So at least Mrs. Plavsic is referring to the same word used by Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For what it's worth, I'm just noting that [B/C/S spoken] is used by Mrs. Plavsic, and that's not precisely the formulation used in Mr. Buha's remarks. I have no idea whether that's -- that makes a difference, but it is a small distinction that may be worth noting. I leave that to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's not exactly the same but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We could have the two very short passages done by the interpreters, Your Honour. That will probably solve everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Mr. Sladojevic would read the first line where Mrs. Plavsic is speaking. Slowly read it, please, Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. [Interpretation] "I think we should adopt the remarks of Mr. Aleksa Buha, namely to introduce into the material at any cost the term 'union of states.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the last sentence spoken by Mr. Buha.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Therefore, we should insist that as far as the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned, the only possibilities -- the only possibility is to have national republics, individually speaking, and at the level of the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina a union of independent republics or states nation based or national in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been clarified. And then I'd also like to know whether the same words are used in the -- a couple of lines upwards where the English starts: "The first real name to be expressed." If you could find that, Mr. Sladojevic, because there we find a similar expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The first thing that should be called by its real name is that this Bosnia and Herzegovina in its present borders can only be a union of independent ethnic republics of the Serbian, Croatian, and Muslim peoples."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having verified this, please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Krajisnik, if we go to page 51, and it's page 34 in the English. Mr. Koljevic announces, "We just received an invitation from Mr. Cutileiro to continue the conference on the coming Monday and Tuesday," which is going to be the 16th and 17th of March, "and his appeal to us contains the Declaration (American European) on the recognition of the Yugoslav republics. I shall read the translation to you." I'm not proposing to read all that out unless I'm asked to, but it includes after the various numbered points in this context it concludes the statement or request coming from the European Community: "In this context all sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina are invited to accept without delay the EC's proposals on a constitutional order which will enable the peaceful and harmonious development of this republic within its existing borders. "The EC and the USA have also agreed to oppose strongly any efforts -- any effort endangering the stability and territorial integrity of these two republics." The -- there are a number of other points in between, but let's go straight to -- from there, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 77, which is page 50 in the English. And then Mr. Milanovic, as the -- formally the chairman, it's clear, Mr. Krajisnik, in effect he's handing over the floor and the effective chair to you. That really doesn't come from this text. He says -- he hands it over to you and you say, "I should like to inform you that the working group has drawn up a document which I shall read out and then put to the vote. "Let us try to do some conclusions. "Conclusions. First, I should like to ask all the deputies to vote on the EC's proposal entitled Statement of Principles for New Constitutional Arrangements in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Who is for? "The Assembly unanimously rejected the document of the European Community entitled Statement of Principles for New Constitutional Arrangements In Bosnia and Herzegovina. "The deputies then adopted the proposal of the President of the Assembly, Mr. Krajisnik, and individually declared themselves in respect of this document. All were against (see list of names as annex.)" Did that, by the end of this meeting then -- or near the end of this meeting, Mr. Krajisnik, did that come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could see here on page 76 that the entire debate was led by Mr. Milanovic, and the two of us swapped roles here. He asked me to read out the conclusions of the working group that had been established, and I read them out. And when you see this sentence, "Who is in favour of this material," that's something that he said. And then he noted that everybody was against. To us this was a negative development, because if you reject a certain paper, then how can you go to negotiate, whereas we had already received announcement of continued negotiations. That's why I suggested the following conclusion here below as the person sitting next to Mr. Milanovic. We're looking at minutes here, so it's difficult to establish who proposed it for voting. I was not very happy with it. I wanted everybody to vote individually. And then if everybody votes no, that means everybody was against the peace plan. If you want me to comment it any further, I can. I intervened here as an assistant, as a helper to Mr. Milanovic, because I wasn't chairing the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- the point of my questions here is not really who was technically or effectively chairing the Assembly, but that's -- so bearing that in mind, you then, the president, Mr. Krajisnik, made the following proposals: "To authorise the representatives previously authorised by the Assembly of the Serbian People to continue negotiations with the two other ethnic communities - the Muslims and the Croats - in the presence of the EC, subject to the following restrictions: "The minimum below which the negotiators must not go in representing the interests of the Serbian people are the results of the plebiscite or a confederal set-up of BH which entails three sovereign national states which may be linked up on the confederal principle." So, Mr. Krajisnik, you were -- is it correct that both limbs of that proposal came from you here at this point, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It's not correct. Those conclusions that were proposed above were developed by the working group, and I was asked by the chairman, I didn't chair the session, I was asked by the chairman to read them out as he normally reads such conclusions when I chair the sessions, and they were rejected. Now, after they rejected the conclusions, I suggested this not as the chairman but as the person sitting next to the chairman. And I had made this suggestion to rescue the negotiations, to enable us to continue. Maybe the interpretation is wrong, but it can be understood from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we clearly we haven't got to the substance of this question, and bearing in mind what Your Honour said earlier about the need for a little time at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next question is bound to take a little time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing so, perhaps, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps to think it over overnight. I see a little bit later in the same minutes, I see that you're asking Mr. Ostojic to read something out which seems to swap general the situation on who was presiding but it's perhaps not that vital, but if there would be any explanation for that, please give it to us tomorrow. We have a few procedural issues -- yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you please, could you just look at the previous page where Krajisnik takes the floor. "I inform you that the working group has drafted the paper that I will read out to you so that you can state your opinion whether we are going to accept it." So I'm talking about the working group and presenting their conclusions when the chairman gives me the floor. And after the voting, I did make another contribution. You're right on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we now move to the procedural issues. First of all, I'll just find them. Yes, some deadlines that are expiring today. Double pension legislation. I do see that on the 25th of April the parties agreed that they would get back on the 9th of May; and we do know that the Defence has sent this legislation to the CLSS on the 27th of April. Therefore, I wonder what to expect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know that the CLSS have submitted some documents to us. A member of our team told me earlier he was having trouble accessing their website, so I don't know the answer. I will find out for tomorrow and I will report back, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you. Then the Neilsen source material. The material was submitted on the 25th of April, and the Defence were supposed to come back with any objections by May the 9th, which is today, and still the day is young, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Clearly I'm not, Your Honour, but day is. Your Honour, we had appreciated, in fact we had mentioned we needed a couple of minutes for precisely that point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear, yes. As I said, the day is young.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the day is young. What we were going to ask, Your Honour, is that we might have until tomorrow to make our filing on that. We had three members of the team working on it today, Your Honour. We just haven't managed to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any strong objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Nothing too strong, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have until tomorrow, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there's one issue I'd like to raise briefly in private session. Could we turn into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, then you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That took us by surprise. I thought it would take until 7.00. The --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. The two limbs the proposal which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- I thought you would like to raise an issue I mentioned before. I said that there was -- whether there were any objections against -- what was it? Oh, no, no. You said that Neilsen source material you would like to have until tomorrow. Yes. You first said that that is exactly what I would like to address later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, took me by surprise. I wasn't expecting to continue any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. I thought that there was still something to be raised. So it was the one-day extension.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the day is young, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, we conclude for the day. I again remind you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony given or still to be given, and we'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, courtroom II, quarter past 2.00.
